messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Non-binary
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Conflict: Confrontations, Others Cycling: People cycling
  Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nikhil Rao is a 46-year-old non-binary South Asian American software engineer who came to treatment after months of telling themself they should be able to “just get on with it” and finding that they could not. They are married and live with their spouse in a dense urban neighborhood where biking commuters, crowded sidewalks, and public friction are part of ordinary daily life. The event they circle around in therapy began during what had been an unremarkable afternoon. Nikhil had been outside near a busy street when a police encounter escalated quickly and physically. In the confusion there were raised voices, bodies moving too fast, the sense of being singled out and overpowered, and an immediate conviction that they were no longer safe in a world they had assumed had rules. What remains most vivid is not a tidy sequence but fragments of confrontation: a uniform, sharp commands, the proximity of strangers, the shock of being handled violently in public while other people watched.

Since then, Nikhil has struggled to make the event into a clear narrative. Even alone, trying to describe it to themself, the story breaks apart. They can begin with where they were and that there was police violence, but then the thread disappears. At times the emotional force of the event arrives all at once—terror, humiliation, helplessness—without any image attached to it. It can happen in the middle of a workday, when they are reviewing code, and for a few moments they are flooded with the same intensity they felt then, though they could not say exactly what they are remembering. If they do get close to recalling more, they notice themself mentally veering away before the memory feels complete, as if some inner brake is pulled and the rest cannot be reached.

The triggers that unsettle Nikhil would have seemed bizarre to them before this happened. Confrontation is the most obvious. If voices sharpen in a meeting, if a stranger on the train platform argues with someone, if their spouse sounds suddenly angry during an ordinary disagreement, Nikhil’s body reacts before they can reason with it. Their chest tightens, their muscles tense, and they become acutely aware of exits, corners, and anyone standing too close. But what troubles them almost as much is being caught off guard when they are happy. They have noticed that feeling relaxed on a good evening with their spouse, laughing over dinner, or enjoying a rare easy moment can bring a jolt of alarm. The shift into pleasure feels unsafe, as though letting their guard down is exactly when harm can come. They describe a reflexive thought that happiness is careless, that calm is when people get blindsided.

Their neighborhood and job give these reactions constant places to land. On the walk from the train to the office, cyclists stream past in bike lanes and cut across crosswalks. The sight of people cycling—helmets, wheels flashing past, sudden movement at the edge of vision—can send a shock through Nikhil’s body that feels wildly disproportionate and yet immediate. In the office cafeteria they do not sit casually anymore. They scan the room and choose a seat with protection behind them, ideally facing the door and away from foot traffic. In conference rooms they arrive early enough to avoid being trapped in the middle. They say it is simply practical, but they also know they are always calculating who is nearby, who looks agitated, who might turn unpredictable. They watch other people closely, reading posture, tone, and movement for signs of danger. A teammate slamming a laptop shut, a security guard speaking sharply in the lobby, two men arguing near the bike racks—each can pull Nikhil into the same alert state.

Over time, these habits have altered the texture of their life. At work they have become less spontaneous, less willing to stay for group lunches or celebratory gatherings where they cannot control where they sit. Their spouse has noticed that even pleasant weekends are managed around routes, exits, and avoiding tense public scenes. Nikhil feels ashamed of this and also certain that their caution is justified. They have come to believe that the basic structure of the world is not what they once thought. What was shattered for them was the idea that decency, innocence, or predictability offered any protection. They are certain now that you can never know who will harm you. A uniform no longer signifies safety; neither does a familiar street, a normal afternoon, or a cheerful mood.

Another painful belief has settled in alongside this. Nikhil often feels exposed, as if what happened is somehow visible on their face or body. In meetings or in line for coffee, if someone looks at them for a beat too long, they wonder whether the person can tell. They do not mean that others literally know the details, but that they can see a damagedness, a mark. By the time they sought help, what finally pushed them was not one dramatic collapse but the accumulation of these moments: the impossibility of relaxing without fear, the strain of scanning every room, the way a trivial confrontation could make their body feel seized from the inside. They came in wanting, above all, to be able to exist in ordinary life without feeling ambushed by it, and fearing that if nothing changed they would keep shrinking their world around the possibility of being harmed again.
